title: Cardiovascular Medications: Blood Pressure, Angina, Heart Failure and Bedside Safety
html:
Cardiovascular medications alter vascular tone, circulating volume, cardiac rate, conduction, contractility, remodeling, or renal and hormonal signals. Safe nursing care begins with the treatment goal and the client's current perfusion—not with a memorized blood-pressure cutoff. The RN connects symptoms, posture, vital-sign trends, rhythm, fluid status, kidney function, electrolytes, interacting medications, and the expected time course before and after every dose.

Learning goals

  • Link major cardiovascular medication classes to their physiologic effects.
  • Perform a focused pre-administration assessment based on indication and risk.
  • Recognize hypotension, bradycardia, electrolyte disturbance, kidney injury, angioedema, and toxicity.
  • Use nitrates safely and identify dangerous phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor interactions.
  • Distinguish symptom-relief medications from therapies that improve long-term heart-failure outcomes.
  • Evaluate response using perfusion, function, symptoms, fluid status, laboratory trends, and adverse effects.

Treat the client and the indication—not one number

The same medication may be prescribed for hypertension, angina, dysrhythmia, heart failure, kidney protection, or another condition. Before administration, verify the indication, current order, last dose, blood pressure and trend, heart rate and rhythm, orthostatic symptoms, perfusion, respiratory status, edema, weight and intake/output when relevant, renal function, electrolytes, concurrent medications, and the client's response to prior doses.

Follow client-specific parameters and organizational policy. An isolated reading can be misleading because of cuff size, position, pain, anxiety, activity, or technique. Validate an unexpected measurement when the client is stable, but do not delay escalation for shock, chest pain, acute neurologic change, pulmonary edema, or another dangerous presentation.

Renin–angiotensin system medications

Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors reduce formation of angiotensin II and aldosterone. Angiotensin receptor blockers block angiotensin II signaling. Angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors combine angiotensin-receptor blockade with increased natriuretic-peptide activity. These therapies may reduce blood pressure, afterload, sodium retention, and pathologic remodeling.

Monitor blood pressure, renal function, potassium, volume status, and symptoms. ACE inhibitors commonly cause cough and can cause angioedema; ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and ARNIs can contribute to hyperkalemia, hypotension, and worsening kidney function in susceptible clients. Facial, tongue, or airway swelling is an emergency even if the blood pressure is normal.

ACE inhibitor and ARNI require separation
Sacubitril/valsartan must not be given concurrently with an ACE inhibitor and requires the prescribed 36-hour separation when switching to or from an ACE inhibitor. Verify the medication history and last dose rather than assuming the transition occurred.

Medications acting on the renin–angiotensin system may cause fetal harm. Verify pregnancy-related precautions and notify the prescriber according to the drug, indication, and current clinical situation.

Beta blockers slow adrenergic drive

Beta blockers reduce heart rate, conduction, contractility, and renin release to varying degrees. They are used for selected clients with hypertension, ischemic heart disease, dysrhythmia, and heart failure. Check heart rate, rhythm, blood pressure, perfusion, symptoms, and ordered parameters. Review whether the client has acute decompensation, conduction disease, bronchospastic disease, or interacting rate-slowing medications.

Watch for symptomatic bradycardia, hypotension, dizziness, fatigue, heart block, worsening perfusion, or bronchospasm. Beta blockers can blunt tachycardia during hypoglycemia, although sweating and neuroglycopenic symptoms may remain. Do not stop chronic beta-blocker therapy abruptly unless directed; sudden withdrawal can worsen ischemia, hypertension, or tachyarrhythmia.

Calcium-channel blockers are not one uniform group

Dihydropyridines such as amlodipine primarily vasodilate and may cause headache, flushing, dizziness, and peripheral edema. Non-dihydropyridines such as diltiazem and verapamil also slow atrioventricular conduction and can reduce heart rate and contractility.

Before a rate-slowing calcium-channel blocker, assess pulse, rhythm, blood pressure, symptoms, and concurrent beta blocker or other conduction-slowing therapy. Report symptomatic bradycardia, heart block, hypotension, or worsening heart failure. Peripheral edema from a vasodilator does not automatically mean total-body volume overload; assess weight, lung sounds, jugular venous findings, function, and the overall pattern.

Diuretics change volume and electrolytes

Loop and thiazide-type diuretics increase sodium and water excretion at different nephron sites. Potassium-sparing diuretics and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists reduce potassium loss but can cause hyperkalemia. Nursing assessment includes blood pressure, orthostatic symptoms, weight trend, edema, lung sounds, intake/output, renal function, sodium, potassium, magnesium, and the treatment goal.

Loop diuretics may contribute to hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hyponatremia, volume depletion, kidney injury, and—at high exposure or rapid IV administration—ototoxicity. Thiazide-type agents can also affect sodium, potassium, uric acid, and glucose. Spironolactone and related agents can cause hyperkalemia, especially with kidney dysfunction, potassium supplements, salt substitutes, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or ARNIs.

Schedule and teach diuretics to support adherence and safety while following the prescription. Sudden weight gain, increasing edema, orthopnea, reduced urine output, hypotension, weakness, palpitations, or confusion can signal worsening disease or therapy complications.

Nitrates reduce myocardial workload and relieve ischemic symptoms

Nitroglycerin and other nitrates dilate veins and, at some doses, arteries. Before administration, assess the chest discomfort, blood pressure, heart rate, level of consciousness, recent nitrate doses, volume status, and use of phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors or soluble guanylate-cyclase stimulators. These combinations can cause profound hypotension.

For sublingual nitroglycerin, have the client sit or lie safely, follow the prescribed administration and emergency plan, and reassess pain, pressure, blood pressure, heart rate, and associated symptoms. Headache and flushing can occur, but persistent or worsening chest discomfort, dyspnea, diaphoresis, syncope, dysrhythmia, or hemodynamic instability requires urgent escalation. Never delay emergency evaluation simply because a nitrate dose is available.

Transdermal products require correct placement, removal of the old patch, rotation of sites, and the prescribed nitrate-free interval when ordered to reduce tolerance. Prevent medication transfer and document location and time.

Heart failure therapy has different purposes

For heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, guideline-directed therapy commonly combines an ARNI, ACE inhibitor, or ARB; an evidence-based beta blocker; a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist; and an SGLT2 inhibitor when appropriate. Diuretics primarily relieve congestion. Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate and other medications may be prescribed for selected clients. The regimen is individualized to heart-failure type, symptoms, kidney function, potassium, blood pressure, comorbidities, tolerance, access, and goals.

Do not judge long-term therapy only by whether the client immediately feels different. Evaluate functional capacity, dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, daily weight, hospitalization risk, blood pressure, heart rate, renal function, potassium, adherence, and adverse effects. During acute decompensation, medication changes require coordinated clinical judgment; do not independently hold or continue chronic therapy without using current parameters and escalation pathways.

SGLT2 inhibitors require heart-failure as well as glucose thinking

SGLT2 inhibitors may be prescribed for heart failure or kidney protection even without diabetes. Monitor volume status, renal function, genital or urinary symptoms, and symptoms of ketoacidosis. Ketoacidosis can occur with only modest glucose elevation, especially during acute illness, fasting, surgery, dehydration, or reduced insulin.

Follow prescribed sick-day and peri-procedure plans. Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing, unusual fatigue, or altered mentation warrants assessment rather than reassurance based on a glucose value alone.

Digoxin has a narrow safety margin

Digoxin can increase contractility and slow atrioventricular conduction. Dose and toxicity risk are influenced by age, lean body weight, renal clearance, electrolytes, interacting medications, and clinical condition. Before administration, assess apical pulse and rhythm for the required duration, blood pressure and perfusion, renal function, potassium and magnesium, symptoms, and ordered parameters.

Possible toxicity includes anorexia, nausea, vomiting, confusion, weakness, visual disturbance, bradycardia, conduction changes, or other dysrhythmias. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia can increase myocardial sensitivity, while impaired renal function can prolong exposure. A serum digoxin level must be timed and interpreted with the last dose, clinical findings, renal function, and electrolytes; one number does not override toxicity cues.

Vasodilators and centrally acting medications

Hydralazine and other direct vasodilators may cause headache, reflex tachycardia, fluid retention, or hypotension. Alpha-1 blockers can cause marked first-dose or orthostatic hypotension. Central alpha-2 agonists can cause sedation, dry mouth, and bradycardia; abrupt withdrawal of clonidine can produce severe rebound hypertension.

Teach slow position changes, fall precautions, home monitoring technique, and the danger of stopping certain medications suddenly. Assess adherence barriers without blame: cost, complex schedules, adverse effects, health literacy, transportation, and competing priorities can all alter cardiovascular risk.

Recognize urgent adverse patterns

  • Shock or symptomatic hypotension: altered mentation, syncope, cool skin, weak pulses, chest discomfort, reduced urine output, or severe dizziness with low pressure.
  • Symptomatic bradycardia or block: dizziness, syncope, hypotension, chest discomfort, dyspnea, or poor perfusion with a slow rhythm.
  • Angioedema: lip, tongue, face, throat, or airway swelling after an ACE inhibitor, ARB, or ARNI.
  • Electrolyte toxicity: weakness, confusion, cramps, paresthesia, or dysrhythmia with potassium, sodium, or magnesium change.
  • Worsening heart failure: increasing dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, rapid weight gain, crackles, reduced activity tolerance, or poor perfusion.
  • Digoxin toxicity: gastrointestinal, neurologic, visual, and rhythm findings in the setting of susceptible physiology.

Stop or hold the suspected medication when indicated by the order or protocol, assess ABCs and perfusion, obtain help, place the client on appropriate monitoring, review recent doses and interacting drugs, and communicate objective findings. Do not treat a monitor value in isolation or independently prescribe a corrective medication.

Teaching makes long-term therapy safer

Teach the medication name and purpose, schedule, home blood-pressure and pulse technique when ordered, daily weight method for heart failure, position changes, adherence, missed-dose instructions, interactions, pregnancy precautions, and symptoms requiring urgent help. Avoid recommending potassium supplements or salt substitutes without review because the safe choice depends on the medication and kidney function.

Ask for teach-back: “Show me how you will check your blood pressure,” “Which symptom means you should call emergency services?” and “Which medication should not be taken with your nitrate?” Written medication lists should include dose, timing, indication, and changes after transitions of care.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify indication, symptoms, posture, blood pressure and trend, pulse and rhythm, perfusion, respiratory and fluid status, kidney function, electrolytes, pregnancy considerations, recent doses, and interactions.
  2. Analyze cues: Connect the medication's effect with hypotension, bradycardia, volume change, electrolyte abnormality, kidney injury, ischemia, congestion, or toxicity.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Shock, acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary edema, severe bradycardia or block, angioedema, dangerous dysrhythmia, and major electrolyte disturbance require urgent action.
  4. Generate solutions: Validate data, use client-specific parameters, prevent falls, adjust timing through the prescribed plan, obtain monitoring, clarify interactions, and escalate.
  5. Take action: Withhold an unsafe dose as authorized, support ABCs, activate emergency care, reconcile transitions, administer accurately, and teach with teach-back.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess symptoms, perfusion, function, pressure and rhythm, respiratory and fluid status, weight, urine output, renal function, electrolytes, adverse effects, and adherence.

Clinical example

A client with heart failure is due for a beta blocker, loop diuretic, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. The client reports dizziness when standing; blood pressure is lower than baseline, pulse is 48/min, weight has fallen rapidly, oral intake is poor, creatinine has risen, and potassium is elevated. The RN recognizes a cluster of bradycardia, possible volume depletion, kidney dysfunction, and hyperkalemia rather than administering all scheduled medications automatically. The RN ensures fall safety, repeats and validates vital signs, performs focused perfusion and fluid assessment, reviews trends and recent doses, holds medications according to current parameters, and promptly communicates for a revised plan. Reassessment determines whether perfusion, rhythm, renal function, potassium, and symptoms improve.

Original educational synthesis. Cardiovascular medication selection, dosing, withholding parameters, monitoring, and emergency response require current prescriptions, product labeling, laboratory and rhythm data, pharmacy resources, organizational policy, and qualified clinical supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, continuing education, or an official NCSBN product.
